Define \(\mathfrak{s}\) as the splitting number: the least cardinality of a family \(\mathcal{S}\) of infinite subsets of \(\omega\) such that every infinite \(X\subseteq\omega\) is split by some \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), meaning both \(|X\cap S|=\omega\) and \(|X\setminus S|=\omega\).

Unpack the notation \(\binom{\mathfrak{s}}{\omega}\to\binom{\mathfrak{s}}{\omega}^{1,1}_2\) using Definition 1.1: for every coloring \(c:\mathfrak{s}\times\omega\to 2\), there are \(A\subseteq\mathfrak{s}\) and \(B\subseteq\omega\) with \(|A|=\mathfrak{s}\) and \(|B|=\omega\) such that \(c\restriction(A\times B)\) is constant.
Make clear that the question is about the borderline case \(\lambda=\mathfrak{s}\), not the easier regime \(\lambda<\mathfrak{s}\) covered by Theorem 2.6.
Do not add any regularity or cofinality assumption on \(\mathfrak{s}\); the paper does not build such an assumption into Problem 3.5.
refined_question: Is it relatively consistent with ZFC that the splitting number \(\mathfrak{s}\) - the least size of a family \(\mathcal{S}\) of infinite subsets of \(\omega\) such that every infinite \(X\subseteq\omega\) is split by some \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), i.e. both \(|X\cap S|=\omega\) and \(|X\setminus S|=\omega\) - satisfies \(\mathfrak{s}<\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}\), and nevertheless the strong polarized relation \(\binom{\mathfrak{s}}{\omega}\to\binom{\mathfrak{s}}{\omega}^{1,1}_2\) holds, meaning that every coloring \(c:\mathfrak{s}\times\omega\to 2\) admits \(A\subseteq\mathfrak{s}\) and \(B\subseteq\omega\) with \(|A|=\mathfrak{s}\), \(|B|=\omega\), and \(c\restriction(A\times B)\) constant?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 3, Problem 3.5 exactly, not a broader neighboring question. Definition 1.1 in Section 1 gives the precise meaning of the arrow notation. The nearby background in Theorem 2.6 explains why \(\mathfrak{s}\) is the critical threshold: below the splitting number one gets positive relations under a cofinality condition, so the paper isolates the unresolved borderline case at \(\lambda=\mathfrak{s}\). The surrounding discussion in Section 3 also shows why the inequality \(\mathfrak{s}<\mathfrak{c}\) is the intended extra feature: the known positive model mentioned there has \(\mathfrak{u}<\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{c}\), and Problem 3.5 asks for the 'opposite point of view,' namely separating \(\mathfrak{s}\) from \(\mathfrak{c}\) while retaining the positive relation.
